candidates.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
candidates.author: Italo Calvino
candidates.locator: definition 6, in The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986
candidates.whyThisMonth: In a month of things passing, Calvino names the one made object that keeps giving itself back: a book you can reread all your life and never use up.

candidates.quote: Listen to this reed how it complains: it is telling a tale of separations.
candidates.author: Rumi
candidates.locator: Book I, line 1, the opening line
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous opening in Persian poetry starts with a cut reed singing about having been cut, which is the gentlest way to admit at six in the morning that everything here has been parted from something.

candidates.quote: As they step into the same rivers, other and still other waters flow upon them.
candidates.author: Heraclitus
candidates.locator: Fragment B12 in Diels and Kranz, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker
candidates.whyThisMonth: Not the slogan that nobody steps in the same river twice, but what Heraclitus actually left: the river holds its name and its shape, and that is exactly why the water is free to keep leaving.

candidates.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
candidates.author: Horace
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month's boldest answer to its own elegies: a poet betting in 23 BCE that the poem would outlast the bronze, and a reader proving him right over breakfast two thousand years later.

candidates.quote: The world of dew / Is the world of dew, / And yet . . . / And yet . . .
candidates.author: Kobayashi Issa
candidates.work: The Year of My Life (Oraga Haru)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The whole month in four lines: the teaching about impermanence is accepted, and then quietly not accepted, which is how anyone actually meets a morning after a loss.

candidates.quote: As firmly cemented clam shells / Fall apart in autumn, / So I must take to the road again, / Farewell, my friends.
candidates.author: Matsuo Bashō
candidates.work: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last words of the great travel book turn a parting into a departure: what was firmly cemented comes apart in autumn, and the answer is to walk on and say goodbye warmly.

candidates.quote: Switzerland is a country where very few things begin, but many things end.
candidates.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
candidates.work: The Notebooks of F. Scott Fitzgerald
candidates.locator: section E, Epigrams, Wise Cracks and Jokes, entry 335, Bruccoli edition of 1978
candidates.whyThisMonth: A wry side door into the theme: some places, and some seasons, are simply where things finish, and saying it lightly at six in the morning takes the dread out of it.

candidates.quote: Should auld acquaintance be forgot, / And never brought to mind?
candidates.author: Robert Burns
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 2, The Scots Musical Museum, volume V, number 413, 1796
candidates.whyThisMonth: The question half the world has sung without once hearing it, and on a month about passing things it is the kindest one to wake up to.
